0.content:
Krsnik Noc (also: Krsnik Night, Kresnik Night, Ice Hearth Festival): Krsnik Noc is a festival celebrated in Snezhnaya. Canon gives no details of what it involves. The one known remark is from Ivanovich, a Snezhnayan merchant in Liyue Harbor: during Lantern Rite the glow of the Xiao Lanterns reminded him of it.

He called it "our Krsnik Noc" and, feeling the same warmth in a foreign city, urged the Traveler to visit Snezhnaya and join one of its festivals. That is the full extent of what canon says. Nothing in the game through Version 7.1, including the Snezhnaya content, states its date, origin, rituals or meaning.

Practice: No practices are established. The only inference from canon is the mood Ivanovich ties to it: lit lanterns in the night, and an impression of warmth and communal celebration that reminded him of home. Treat everything else as unwritten.

Ivanovich's comparison is the sole in-game reference, made during the Lantern Rite event, which began in Version 1.3. That is why the festival is dated to 1.3 here. Its Chinese name translates as the Ice Hearth Festival, and the French and Russian names also say "icy furnace" or "ice hearth". Treat these as clues to naming only, not as evidence of what the festival does.

Regional variation: Canon records no regional variation, and nothing places the festival in a particular Snezhnayan city. It is described only as Snezhnayan. No Nod-Krai (6.x) or 7.0-7.1 source found describes it either.

Scene use: Use it lightly. A Snezhnayan character can mention it with homesick fondness, comparing lanterns, firelight or a warm crowd on a cold night to it, as Ivanovich does. Keep details vague or let the speaker be vague. Do not invent a canonical date, ritual, food, song or origin story and present it as fact.

If a scene needs specifics, make it clear the speaker is describing their own family or town custom, not a universal rule. Characters who are not Snezhnayan should know it only by name or by what a traveller told them.

1.content:
Snezhnaya Cuisine (also: Snezhnayan cuisine, Snezhnayan food, Snezhnaya food, Snezhnayan dishes): Snezhnayan cooking is hearty, warming food built for a land of eternal winter, and it clearly echoes Slavic cuisines. Staples are rye bread, smetana (sour cream), beetroot borscht, cold soups, grilled skewers, thinly shaved frozen fish and cured sausage. The drink everyone mentions is Fire-Water, a famously potent spirit; downing a whole glass in one go is the respectful norm. Dairy, preserved meat and seafood from coastal towns matter more than fresh produce.

The cuisine became detailed in game with Version 7.0, when Snezhnograd gained the Podvorye Restaurant and a set of regional dishes with item text describing how they are made and eaten. Before that it was known mostly through Tartaglia's remarks and the Fire-Water anecdotes told in Mondstadt.

Practice: Climate shapes the table. Wheat is hard to grow in the cold, so rye serves in its place (rye bread, rye flour), and some milk is turned into smetana rather than ordinary cream. Seaside regions eat mostly seafood, according to Tartaglia's character story as summarised by the wiki; whether the rest of the country does is not stated. Dishes named in canon:
- Borscht: a red beetroot soup, slow-simmered in stages, finished with a spoonful of sour cream; the item text says it keeps the bitter cold at bay. Tartaglia calls it authentic and says he can make it from specialty ingredients of his hometown.
- Snowrealm Okroshkas: a cold soup of cooked ingredients under a sour-cream broth. Some Snezhnayans down a large bowl in one go on the coldest days to prove they can defeat the cold.
- Stroganina: raw frozen fish shaved into thin curling strips with a sharp blade and served with coarse salt, a common cold platter.
- Snezhnaya Shashliks: marinated meat grilled on iron skewers over coals, eaten at courtyard gatherings, on hunts, or on a patch of cleared snow wherever a fire can be lit.
- Glupov Rye Bread: a dense, long-fermented loaf that keeps well, a common ration for travelling merchants, soldiers and hunters.
- Medovik: a layered honey cake with sour-cream frosting.
- Podvorye Smoked Sausage: sliced smoked sausage, a signature dish of the Podvorye Restaurant that nobody at the table turns down.
- Kvass: a mildly fizzy, alcohol-free drink with a sour rye-bread aroma, sold at the Kvasnik beverage shop and described as a drink no Snezhnayan would refuse.

Fire-Water is the national spirit. Tartaglia says most people love it, and that anyone who will stand out in the cold with you drinking it and talking has earned your complete trust (he adds that such a person is the kind you want on the battlefield). Draining the entire glass in one go is customary and counts as showing respect (open-world NPC and Ororon's story). A Dawn Winery anecdote told by the Mondstadt NPC Vile shows the cost to outsiders: during a banquet for a Snezhnayan diplomatic and merchant party, Diluc followed the custom, emptied his glass of Fire-Water, then slept for three days and refused the proposed partnership, saying Mondstadt's people could not handle it. In Snezhnograd a hidden exploration objective has the Traveler waking a drunk named Vanya, who is repeatedly found passed out by the restaurant district after too much Fire-Water.

Regional variation: Seaside Snezhnaya leans on seafood. Nod-Krai, nominally Snezhnayan but warmer and more independent, has its own cooking: the Meat-Filled Rye Bun, a fish-and-bacon filling baked inside thick rye dough and sold in Nasha Town, is classed as a Nod-Krai dish and the in-game rye ingredient lists Nod-Krai as a source. See the Nod-Krai cuisine entry for that region. Fae and Volkodlak communities keep their own tables, as the Podvorye shows.

Camaraderie at the table is part of Snezhnayan culture generally: the Culture page notes closeness to family and a habit of building trust through shared drinking in the cold. Outsiders in Mondstadt and Liyue know the cuisine mostly through Fire-Water and Fatui diplomats.

Scene use: Use Snezhnayan meals to convey warmth against cold: a bowl of borscht with a spoonful of smetana, a chunk of heavy rye bread, skewers sizzling over coals in a snowy yard, or a shot of Fire-Water drained in one swallow to show respect. A host who offers Fire-Water expects the guest to finish the glass. Do not invent specific recipes, prices or feast traditions beyond the item texts.

Contrast settings: a Snezhnograd restaurant with fae and Volkodlak staff and polite service; a soldier's or hunter's field meal of rye bread and skewers; a coastal fishing town's seafood table; a Nod-Krai bakery stall with fish-stuffed rye. A Mondstadter or Liyuean guest is likely to find Fire-Water overpowering. Treat the alcohol-free Kvass as a reasonable choice for anyone who declines.

Examples: Borscht (red beet soup with sour cream), Snowrealm Okroshkas (cold sour-cream soup), Stroganina (shaved frozen fish with salt), Snezhnaya Shashliks (grilled skewers), Glupov Rye Bread (long-fermented rye loaf), Medovik (layered honey cake), Podvorye Smoked Sausage, Kvass (non-alcoholic rye drink) and Fire-Water (potent spirit).

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1 the cuisine is a stable, fully documented tradition in Snezhnograd with dishes, shops and recipes; no story event changes it. Fire-Water remains the national spirit.

2.content: Fire-Water is Snezhnaya's best-known alcoholic drink, described as an extremely strong blend. Tartaglia holds that drinking it and talking with someone out in the cold builds complete trust. Emptying a full glass at once is the polite custom. Diluc did so at a Dawn Winery banquet for Snezhnayan merchants and passed out for three days (Vile's anecdote). The recipe, proof and ingredients are not given in canon.

3.content: A long-established restaurant in Snezhnograd, in front of Snezhnograd Square, offering refined takes on traditional Snezhnayan food and fine Fire-Water. Its owner and whole staff are Volkodlak and fae. The word podvorye means courtyard in Russian. Buturlina serves as its shopkeeper; Tolstaya sells similar fare at the separate Restaurant Zorya.

4.comment: Snezhnaya Cuisine: Special dishes of Vesna and Alyosha
4.content: Gameplay-adjacent flavour. Cooking Snowrealm Okroshkas with Vesna may yield her special dish, Hoarfrost Soup: the item text has her declaring a "secret Vila snow flurry soup", inviting everyone to add what they like, and eating most of it herself after Paimon contributes the ingredients. Cooking Snezhnaya Shashliks with Alyosha may yield The Bullseye Roast, a massive gamey skewer he grills with the same confidence as his marksmanship while Tugarin barks excitedly. Both are portrayal hints about those characters, not general Snezhnayan practice.

5.content:
Daily Life in Snezhnaya (also: Snezhnayan daily life, Life in Snezhnaya, Snezhnayan way of life, Snezhnayan customs): Snezhnaya is the frozen northern nation, and ordinary life there is organised around staying warm. Each city is built around a Kresnik's Torch burning Kresnik Kristall, trains cross the tundra, and the Fatui, the Veche and state bureaus run daily affairs. Loyalty and keeping one's word matter deeply.

Daily routine is shaped by heat, rail travel and the state. Ordinary people are practical and often wry: notices and newspapers show them complaining about scams, queueing for theatre tickets and insuring against train delays. Nod-Krai, in the south, is warmer and looser and is treated separately.

Beneath the routine runs a long squeeze on energy. Project Stuzha, a set of Veche-approved reforms limiting public energy use so power can go to the Armory Palace, has been extended again and again and has left parts of the country in poor shape; villages that depend on kristall deliveries can be cut off. The old order also lingers: Prime Ice art, once a court luxury, is now being opened to the public, and fae and humans share towns whose mixing varies from city to city.

Practice: - **Warmth first.** Blizzards can last a month (Nadia of Liyue) and Tartaglia says you would freeze if you stopped moving outside, so people live indoors in heated towns built around Kresnik's Torches.
- **Values.** Loyalty and plain dealing are prized; a nursery rhyme threatens a pinkie-promise breaker with the ice, and betrayal or an unpaid debt feels like a personal insult.

- **Heat as infrastructure.** The Royal Energy Commission maintains the torches and manages how kristall is shipped and used. Kristall is mined mainly at Novokitezhgrad and sent out by rail. The main torch burns in Kresnik's Burning Heart in Snezhnograd.
- **Trains.** Railways carry people and goods safely across the tundra. The Snezhnaya Royal Railway Transport Bureau staffs the stations; Snezhnograd's Central Station is the largest, and arrivals pass an inspection before taking the lift up into the city.
- **Who runs things.** The Fatui act as army, police and diplomatic corps, the Snezhnograd Veche (a council of interest groups) debates and sets policy, and the Druzhna guard the Tsaritsa. The Adventurers' Guild began in Snezhnaya.
- **Drink.** Fire-Water is the famous strong spirit. Downing a whole glass in one go is normal and respectful, and Tartaglia says drinking and talking together in the cold builds complete trust.

- **Why the torches exist.** Before them the whole land was only frigid or subzero ground, habitable by hardy fae alone; the Belyi Tsar built the torches after he opened his realm to humans. The Fatui keep a debt-collection division.
- **Travel and commuting.** Svetloledovka's Prime Ice miners live in Snezhnograd and commute by train. Morepesok is a fishing station where the biggest catch earns respect. Sretomorozsk, in the southwest, is almost deserted and mostly used by people entering or leaving Nod-Krai. Rankova Zorya is a former temporary stop that someone still maintains.
- **News and notices.** The Snezhnaya Vestnik newspaper is read at stands inside train stations. In Snezhnograd the Veche set up a bulletin board for municipal notices and public messages, between Podvorye Restaurant and the Northland Bank.
- **Eating out.** Podvorye Restaurant serves refined versions of traditional food and good Fire-Water; its owner and staff are all Volkodlak and fae. Coastal people eat mostly seafood (Tartaglia), borscht is called an authentic dish, and rye replaces wheat because wheat grows poorly in the cold.
- **Culture and reading.** The Korolevskiy Theater is described as a holy land for singers and dancers, and tickets are so sought after that the troupe warns the public to buy only from the theatre. Torchlight Books is a Snezhnograd bookshop owned by Moes that takes reader suggestions.
- **Alchemy.** Alchemy is banned on the Snezhnayan mainland, so Snezhnograd, uniquely among the main cities, has no crafting bench.
- **Rules of the cold.** Game text sorts areas into Normal Temperature, Cold, Frigid and Subzero zones (a gameplay abstraction). Towns and train interiors are Normal Temperature Zones. At Svetloledovka a worker named Zhuravlev nearly freezes and recovers beside a portable heat source, thanking the Traveler with Glaciafruit.
- **Kristall supply.** The supply can fail. In Gunfire in the Silent Lands the engineer Shishkin says the village of Alatyr, which has no station, has had its kristall deliveries stop, so everyone could freeze unless something is done. Kristall was first found by following Kristall Bugs.
- **Energy politics.** Per Guiding Notes, Project Stuzha is an umbrella term for time-limited energy policies meant to conserve power for research at the Armory Palace; progress has been slow, costs have soared above projections, and the extensions annoy many people. Many Veche disagreements revolve around it. Arlecchino, Tartaglia, Pulcinella and Pantalone are named as involved, with Pierro behind it. A later bulletin notice says the Veche has resolved to close it in the near future.
- **Class and work.** Zolnyy, the "Ash District" of Snezhnograd, is the industrial quarter. A Vestnik article on a Prime Ice sculpture exhibition quotes a poem from the Pale Star Court era: nobles received sculptures while Zolnyy's miners could not afford a bowl of red beet soup; the Veche and the Prime Ice Art Alliance now present the art as being brought closer to the people. One anonymous poster on the board complains that blacksmiths prioritise Snezhnograd locals for apprenticeships.
- **Fae and humans.** Snowland Fae live among humans: many in Novokitezhgrad, fewer but still a fair number in Snezhnograd. Jack Frosts are common and playful but cannot speak.
- **Civic life.** The Rokot, a civilian political group whose members hide behind codenames, shows people organising outside the Veche.
- **Hazards.** Some areas contain the Shadow Realm. When one is found, the Royal Energy Commission quarantines it and calls the Druzhna; those caught inside rarely come out unchanged.

Regional variation: - **Snezhnograd.** Capital with the Central Station, the Veche State Hall, the Druzhna HQ, Glupov (the Fatui's base, named by Anastasya "the city of fools"), the Adventurers' Guild headquarters and a Statue of The Seven. Flins calls it beautiful, with brilliant night skies and endless blizzards.
- **Novokitezhgrad.** Mining and liquor town southeast of Snezhnograd, with many fae living alongside humans.
- **Svetloledovka.** Prime Ice mining village under the frozen peaks.
- **Morepesok.** Small fishing village and Tartaglia's hometown.
- **Sretomorozsk.** Border town, station and port facing Nod-Krai.

- **Alatyr and small villages.** Settlements without a station depend on deliveries, which makes them vulnerable when the supply chain falters.

Scene use: Open with warmth and travel: a torch glowing over a platform, the Transport Bureau inspection, frost on a window, hot soup. Let NPCs be practical and a little sardonic, quick to name a debt or a promise. Use notices, newspapers and ticket queues for texture. Do not present the Tsaritsa's Edicts or Fatui policy as something every citizen resents or loves.

Cold is a constant: characters pause by heaters, check that deliveries are coming and grumble about energy limits. A Fire-Water toast is a natural way to show trust. Avoid inventing festival rituals, school systems or family customs; canon through 7.1 does not detail them.

Examples: - A commuter boards at Svetloledovka and rides to Snezhnograd for the evening shift.
- A theatre fan has been warned that backstage passes do not exist.
- A fisherwoman at Morepesok brags about her catch.
- A Veche notice announces the close of Project Stuzha.

6.comment: Daily Life in Snezhnaya: Kresnik's Torch and Kresnik Kristall in Daily Life
6.content:
Kresnik's Torches are furnaces burning Kresnik Kristall that keep Snezhnayan towns warm and protect them from snowstorms. Every city is built around one, and small civilian models are placed around the country. The most important is in Kresnik's Burning Heart in Snezhnograd. By the Snezhnayan account the Belyi Tsar built them to let humans make a world of their own in the cold. The Royal Energy Commission oversees the torches and manages how the kristall is shipped and used. Kristall is mined chiefly at Novokitezhgrad and travels by rail.

Kristall is said to come from the authority released by the Cryo Dragon when it lost control about 6,000 years ago, an account from Aksinya and a potion formula in quest text. Early people allegedly found its veins by following Kristall Bugs. Villages without stations, such as Alatyr, suffer when deliveries stop.

7.comment: Daily Life in Snezhnaya: Trains and Stations in Snezhnaya
7.content:
Trains are the lifeline across the tundra, in the loading-screen words the veins of an iron-and-steel nation. The Snezhnaya Royal Railway Transport Bureau runs them, and conductors, ticket agents and safety officers staff the stations. Snezhnograd Central Station is the largest; Svetloledovka's miners commute from the capital; Morepesok serves fisherfolk; Sretomorozsk, nearly deserted, serves those entering or leaving Nod-Krai; Rankova Zorya is a former temporary stop that someone still maintains. Vestnik newspaper stands sit inside stations.

Train interiors are Normal Temperature Zones, so passengers can travel safely without being exposed to the cold. The Traveler's own train, called with the Eye of Graeae, is a separate gameplay convenience and not how ordinary citizens travel.

8.comment: Daily Life in Snezhnaya: Snezhnograd Bulletin Board and the Vestnik
8.content:
Two sources show the tone of public life. The bulletin board in Snezhnograd lets residents read municipal notices and leave messages, and it mixes official Veche resolutions with ticket-scam warnings, pet questions and shop adverts. The Vestnik is a newspaper sold at station stands, running news, advertisements and "Tales of the Strange and Incredible" contributor stories. Its adverts and health columns are in-world opinion and often absurd.

Examples include the Frosta franchise offer, the walking-based Healthguard column, a study against hot baths and Snezhnajoy Insurance. Treat these as satire-tinged colour, not facts about the world.

9.comment: Daily Life in Snezhnaya: Eating and Drinking in Snezhnaya
9.content: Fire-Water is the strong, famous spirit: a full glass in one go is respectful, and drinking and talking in the cold builds trust, per Tartaglia. Borscht is called an authentic dish by Tartaglia and appears at Podvorye Restaurant, a long-established Snezhnograd restaurant run entirely by Volkodlak and fae that serves refined traditional food. Rye replaces wheat, and some milk is made into smetana. See the cuisine entry for detail.

10.comment: Daily Life in Snezhnaya: Project Stuzha and Everyday Energy Limits
10.content:
Project Stuzha is a package of Veche-passed energy reforms that limit public energy use so power can go to the Armory Palace. It has been extended repeatedly, cost far more than expected, and has left parts of Snezhnaya in poor condition. Many Veche arguments revolve around it, and a later Veche notice says it will be formally closed. Details of its purpose and the Harbingers behind it belong to its own entry.

Quest text shows concrete effects, such as the stopped kristall deliveries to Alatyr. The later chapters reveal that Stuzha was a step toward Project Mistilteinn, a weapon for the Tsaritsa's struggle against the Heavenly Principles (spoiler-level minor to major; see the project entry).

11.comment: Daily Life in Snezhnaya: Prime Ice, Zolnyy and Class
11.content: Zolnyy is Snezhnograd's industrial "Ash District". Prime Ice mining happens at Svetloledovka, and a Vestnik article records that in the Pale Star Court era Prime Ice sculptures were a court-only art while Zolnyy's miners could hardly afford soup. The Veche and the Prime Ice Art Alliance now stage a public exhibition as part of a move to bring the art to ordinary people.

12.content:
Snezhnaya and Nod-Krai Fashion (also: Snezhnaya clothing, Snezhnayan attire, Snezhnayan fashion, Nod-Krai clothing, Nod-Krai attire, Fatui uniforms, Lightkeeper uniforms): Snezhnayan and Nod-Krai dress is best known by what marks a person's group. Ordinary people (boys, men, girls and women) wear civilian outfits; bounty hunters have their own look; Fatui members wear standard uniforms marked with the organisation's Palestar emblem; the Frostmoon Scions have moonchanter, priestess and acolyte attire; and the Lightkeepers of Nod-Krai wear ranked uniforms and carry Oath Lanterns.

Canon gives no written description of how Snezhnayans tailor clothes for the cold or what fabrics they use, so scenes should lean on group markers rather than invented detail.

Practice: - Civilians: the wiki distinguishes three boys' outfits, seven men's styles, one girl's outfit and four women's styles, all worn by ordinary NPCs.
- Bounty hunters: three men's outfits and one woman's outfit form a category separate from civilian wear.
- Fatui: standard uniforms for men and for women, plus at least one alternate men's uniform.

- The Fatui emblem, the Palestar Banner, is a stylised filled-in Solomon's knot over a circular emblem. It is typically seen on Fatui masks and clothing and shows the wearer's affiliation.
- Frostmoon Scions: three tiers of dress are listed, moonchanter (worn by Lauma), priestess and acolyte. The Scions say the sacred Hyperborean bloodline carries antler crowns, so antlers may appear on those of that line.
- Lightkeepers: the Starshyna, Ratniki Squad Leaders and ordinary Ratniki (male and female) each have a listed uniform. The order's traditional insignia is a nightingale holding a burning wick in its beak, and every Ratnik must carry an Oath Lantern that lets other Lightkeepers and the Starshyna detect them.

- Rank structure behind the Lightkeeper uniforms: the Starshyna leads, under them are Sergeant Majors (sometimes addressed as Captains), then Squad Leaders, then Ratniki. Nikita is the current Starshyna, having inherited the post from Sigurd.
- Nod-Krai is a mixed region where several groups coexist (Lightkeepers, Frostmoon Scions, the Voynich Guild in Nasha Town, and a Fatui presence), so a crowd there can be read by affiliation markers: Fatui emblem, Lightkeeper lantern, Scion dress.

Regional variation: Mainland Snezhnaya and Nod-Krai are treated together on the source page. Nod-Krai is described as warmer and more independent, and its dress is tied more to the group (Lightkeeper, Scion, Voynich, Fatui) than to a stated regional costume. Whether civilian dress differs between the two is not stated.

Character Cards for Snezhnayan figures use faction emblems (Fatui, Druzhna, Snowland Fae, the Korolevskiy Theater, Zapolyarny Palace). That is a design convention of the game's UI rather than clothing.

Scene use: Signal affiliation with one or two concrete markers: a Fatui mask with the Palestar emblem, a Lightkeeper's Oath Lantern, a Scion's antler crown, a bounty hunter's distinct kit.

Do not invent fabrics, colours or cold-weather gear that canon does not describe. Keep children's clothing plain and practical. Do not give the Lightkeeper insignia to Fatui or vice versa, and do not claim all Frostmoon Scions have antlers; the trait belongs to the pure Hyperborean bloodline.

Examples: - A Ratnik at a Nod-Krai crossroads, Oath Lantern in hand, identified by the lantern as a Lightkeeper.
- A Fatui soldier in uniform with the Palestar emblem on mask or clothing, standing out in a foreign town.
- A priestess and an acolyte of the Frostmoon Scions at a ceremony on Hiisi Island.

13.comment: Snezhnaya and Nod-Krai Fashion: Palestar Banner
13.content: The Palestar Banner is the Fatui's emblem: a stylised, filled-in Solomon's knot on top of another circular emblem. It is typically seen on Fatui masks and clothing and shows who the wearer serves.

14.comment: Snezhnaya and Nod-Krai Fashion: Lightkeeper Uniform and Oath Lantern
14.content: Lightkeepers (Nod-Krai's defenders against the Wild Hunt) have separate uniforms for the Starshyna, Squad Leaders and the Ratniki rank and file, male and female. Their traditional insignia is a nightingale holding a burning wick in its beak. Every Ratnik must carry an Oath Lantern so other Lightkeepers and the Starshyna can detect them.

15.comment: Snezhnaya and Nod-Krai Fashion: Frostmoon Scions Dress
15.content: The Frostmoon Scions of Hiisi Island have named tiers of dress: moonchanter (Lauma's role), priestess and acolyte. The Scions hold that the sacred Hyperborean bloodline carries silver blood, kuuvahki sensitivity, antler crowns said to be a gift of the Frost Moon, and the ability to speak with all living things. The wiki records the dress tiers without describing garments.

16.content:
Religion in Snezhnaya (also: Snezhnayan faith, devotion to the Tsaritsa, worship of the Cryo Archon, Pale Star devotion): Snezhnaya has no known church. Its devotion is aimed at one living person, the Tsaritsa (Anastasya Feodorovna Snezhnaya), Cryo Archon and God of Love, who also rules the nation directly. Loyalists address her with sacral titles ("Holy One of All Winters", "Sovereign of Grace and Absolution") and say that all in Snezhnaya is offered to her throne. Older loyalties survive: the Pale Star of the Belyi Tsar's court, and fae saints and songs. The Tsaritsa herself rejects the "love" her divine office is supposed to carry. Nothing here is a priesthood or a holy calendar; do not invent one.

Faith and politics are the same thing in Snezhnaya. The Fatui, the Druzhna and the nobles serve "Her Majesty" in devotional language, while the Tsaritsa's own stance, as the wiki records it, is closer to refusal than to being worshipped. Her predecessor, the Belyi Tsar, was also God of Love and led the Pale Star Court. The Fatui's Palestar Banner and the Palestar Edict (issued, then rescinded, during the Nod-Krai crisis) have names that echo it; the wiki does not state that they honour him.

Several layers coexist: loyalist devotion to the living Tsaritsa, nostalgia and gratitude among some fae for the Belyi Tsar, Vila reverence for Saint Strivozha, and the separate moon-and-ancestor faith of Nod-Krai. Ordinary Snezhnayans are more often described through loyalty, debt and survival than through prayer.

Practice: Devotion is mostly spoken and civic. People refer to "Her Majesty" with reverence, the Fatui exist to carry out her will, and the Statues of the Seven in Snezhnaya show the Cryo Archon. No regular rites, clergy or temples for her are known.

- Titles. The dedication of the General History of Snezhnaya addresses her as Tsaritsa of All Snezhnaya, Eternal Sovereign Under the Pale Star, Protectress of the Fae Kindreds, Holy One of All Winters, Sovereign of Grace and Absolution and Devoted Bestower of Boundless Grace. This is courtly writing, not a liturgy.
- Offering to the throne. A Snezhnaya loading-screen tip says that in Snezhnaya all shall be offered unto the throne of Her Majesty the Tsaritsa.
- Loyalist speech. The Druzhna officer Akvilina talks of Her Majesty's glory and boundless grace and calls fae bandits traitors. The councillor Golitsyn says he does his duty "in Her Majesty's name", closes with "May Her Majesty's glory endure", and calls fae and humans fuel for Her Majesty's flame.

- Statues of the Seven. The Snezhnayan statues are described as massive, said to be sculpted in the likeness of the Cryo Archon, with an inscription on the harsh winter and on grace that is given to those chosen and earned by the recipient.
- Devotion abroad. Snezhnayans sent overseas, even those who have grown fond of their posting, say they would never betray the Tsaritsa.
- Funeral at the Sanctuary of Grief. After the Harbinger Signora died in Inazuma, the Tsaritsa held a funeral for her at the Sanctuary of Grief, a domed sanctuary in the Everfrozen Earth. After the Harbingers paid their respects (all but the missing Scaramouche) she froze the tomb and the whole mausoleum in thick ice. The wiki notes the building's resemblance to Neo-Byzantine church architecture; that is an observation, not a stated religious function.
- Korolevskiy Theater. A loading-screen tip calls the Korolevskiy Theater a "virtual site of pilgrimage" and holy land for singers and dancers. This is metaphor for artists' devotion, not a shrine of the Archon.
- Oath-like exclamations. Serialised fiction in the Snezhnaya Vestnik has characters say "may Her Majesty preserve my soul" and "His Majesty preserve us".
- Nation of the pinkie promise. Betrayal and unpaid debt are treated as personal affronts, and the nursery rhyme about a broken pinkie promise being thrown on the ice shows a moral code more than a creed.

The tsaritsa and love: The Tsaritsa holds the office of God of Love, as every Cryo Archon has, but she refuses to identify with it. The wiki records (citing the Light and Shadow quest) that the Heavenly Principles laid a curse on the gods requiring them to love humanity, and that she regards any love she feels as false and coerced. In 7.1 she told the Traveler that she needed to understand the nation she is "supposed to love", and appointed them Consultant to the Tsaritsa because she could not be seen to favour any minister. Subordinates such as Vesna and Danica insist she is more sincerely kind than she believes.

Dainsleif's chapter preview describes her as a god with no love left for her people, and no love left for her among them, whose followers hope only to be on her side when she rebels against the divine. Loading screens say many have entrusted their wishes to her in the hope she will raise the banner of rebellion against the heavens. Her aim, the overthrow of the Heavenly Principles, is covered by lore.tsaritsas-plan.

History: The first Cryo Archon was the Belyi Tsar (personal name Monomakh Snezhnyi), God of Love, who led the Snowland Fae from the Pale Star Court and was Cryo Archon from about 2,000 years ago until 500 years ago. He founded Kitezh, the first city, defeated King Miscislav, brought House Strivozha and the Vila under his banner, and later moved his capital to the new Snezhnograd and pardoned humanity. He died in the Cataclysm 500 years ago. The Tsaritsa, who had been a herald of his court, rose to power in its aftermath, demanded that fae princes give up their titles (many died before answering), founded the Snezhnograd Veche and had the Fatui, which she established, build Glupov. Fae lost their monopoly over politics.

Regional variation: - Fae. The Snowland Fae were the aristocracy of the Belyi Tsar. Many now work ordinary jobs, some regret the old order, and loyalist fae like Akvilina denounce those who do. Vila tradition honours Saint Strivozha, "The Pure One", to whom the Songbook quoted in the General History is attributed (it tells the legend of the King of Light, his daughter Koitar and the King of Hyperborea).
- Nod-Krai. This autonomous borderland keeps a different faith centred on the moons and the Moon Maiden, with Moonchanters and the Frostmoon Scions on Hiisi Island. It is covered in culture.nod-krai-religion.

Hymns of the Far North, a hymnbook of the Frostmoon Scions compiled by the priestess Ehrnrooth, contains prayer songs for several figures, including the stranger Saarelainen and the dawnstar goddess Koitar. It is a Nod-Krai text, not a Snezhnayan state creed.

Scene use: Treat Snezhnayan faith as loyalty with a halo. A character may swear by Her Majesty, say "May Her Majesty's glory endure", or keep silent about doubts. Never put a church, bishop or hymn in a Snezhnayan town.

- Druzhna officers and Veche officials talk about the Tsaritsa with reverence.
- A fae character may mention the Belyi Tsar fondly or bitterly; a Vila may mention Saint Strivozha.

Keep knowledge consistent with position. A noble, a Fatui family member, a fae outcast and a Nod-Krai Lightkeeper will not share a view of the Tsaritsa's divinity. Do not give ordinary citizens knowledge of her love-curse or of Saarelainen.

17.comment: Religion in Snezhnaya: The Tsaritsa as Cryo Archon
17.content:
Anastasya Feodorovna Snezhnaya, divine name Vassaga, is the current Cryo Archon and God of Love. She rules Snezhnaya directly from Zapolyarny Palace through Edicts. The Fatui carry out her will, and citizens speak of her in devotional titles. She rejects the divine love she was supposed to feel.

Her regnal title in the General History of Snezhnaya includes "Holy One of All Winters" and "Sovereign of Grace and Absolution".

18.comment: Religion in Snezhnaya: The Belyi Tsar and the Pale Star
18.content: The Belyi Tsar was the first Cryo Archon and God of Love, White Emperor of the Pale Star Court. He united the fae, founded Kitezh and died in the Cataclysm. His Pale Star Court is echoed in the names of the Palestar Banner and Palestar Edict. Some fae remember him as the ruler who granted them amnesty to live with humans.

19.content: Vaselisa von Strivozha, called Saint Strivozha and "The Pure One", led the Vila of House Strivozha after Hyperborea fell and later swore to the Belyi Tsar after losing a duel. The Songbook ascribed to her preserves a legend of the King of Light and his daughter Koitar. The General History of Snezhnaya notes that her true deeds are uncertain.

20.comment: Religion in Snezhnaya: Sanctuary of Grief
20.content: The Sanctuary of Grief is the tomb of the Harbinger Signora, in the Everfrozen Earth. After her death in Inazuma the Tsaritsa held a funeral there, played chess with Pierro using the Anemo and Geo Gnoses, and froze the tomb in thick ice once the Harbingers had paid respects. Its domed architecture resembles Neo-Byzantine churches.

21.content: Krsnik Noc is a Snezhnayan festival mentioned by an NPC during the Lantern Rite. Its meaning and customs are not stated in canon through 7.1.

22.content:
Snezhnayan Ballet and Theater (also: Snezhnayan ballet, Snezhnayan theater, Snezhnayan theatre, Snezhnaya opera and ballet): Snezhnaya's stage arts are centred on the Korolevskiy Troupe and its home, the Korolevskiy Theater in Snezhnograd. The Troupe performs opera, theater and musical shows, and its stars are the prima ballerina Odette and the prima donna Vodyanitsa. Snezhnayans must be coaxed out of their warm homes to attend, but a Troupe poster draws crowds, and the company is especially popular among the Fatui Harbingers and the official Mitya.

The works shown in canon are the ballets Black Snow Swan, The Seabird, The Envoy and The Firebird, plus the family ballet "Spirit Seeker". The Troupe's artists often hold second lives: Odette is a Fatui agent and Vodyanitsa a Water Imp, and both are secretly in the Rokot, so the Theater doubles as a meeting place for people with public and private roles.

The Theater is a working community as much as a venue: an entrance clerk, hosts, a greenroom, a cellar, hunters such as Alyosha taking odd jobs, and critics whose reviews fill the arts pages. Because stage artists in canon also have duties elsewhere, rehearsal schedules repeatedly collide with Fatui work.

Practice: Companies perform in Snezhnograd's Korolevskiy Theater. Stars such as Odette appear on posters, fans queue at the ticket window, and many attend more than once. Ballet is physically severe work: rehearsals at dawn, pointe shoes, a strict diet and constant stretching.

Odette is the model of the discipline. Her rehearsals start early in the morning and she treats each as seriously as a performance. She plans her meals around her work (a hard-boiled egg before going on stage, a real meal afterward) and has a very high pain tolerance. She almost never smiles at audiences, leaves the stage immediately after the curtain, and uses side doors, though autographs and fan meetings are part of the job. Vodyanitsa treats performing as a social art: she rehearses roles aloud, teases colleagues and insists that friends attend her shows.

The Troupe sells tickets at the door. After the Archon Quest Everwinter Without Mercy, the player can buy a ticket from Ksenia and watch one of four short performances that rotate daily; Odette is the focus of at least two of them, with Vodyanitsa onstage or in the wings in others. Audiences differ: Arlecchino, Vesna, Mitya, Sandrone and Tartaglia each attend one. Between shows the Troupe teaches, rehearses, films promotional videos for new ballets, and holds meet-and-greets.

Repertoire: Four ballets are excerpted in the Polestar Ballet Anthology: Black Snow Swan, The Seabird, The Envoy and The Firebird. The Troupe prepares the Black Snow Swan premiere during the World Quest Variations on Belyi and Chernyi, and the Archon Quest chapter Wraith's Nocturne is framed by a preview of "Spirit Seeker". Details appear in the entries below.

The excerpts range from The Firebird (a prince, a flame-feathered bird and a Demon King) to The Envoy (an emperor's dispatch halts a nobleman's banquet) and The Seabird (a composer and a singer meeting again in a country estate). Black Snow Swan is the most symbolic: a black swan, a swan queen and three visiting phantoms.

Regional variation: Snezhnayan theater is shown in Snezhnograd and, in passing, in the mining town of Svetloledovka, where a former Troupe member now works as safety officer and a miner sneers at the Troupe as a fancy opera house. Fontaine and Liyue have their own stage cultures (see Liyue Opera); the sources read make no direct comparison.

Snezhnaya's climate shapes theater-going. Odette's profile notes that coaxing people to an opera house on freezing days takes effort, yet her name on a poster fills the ticket queue. In the Seabird excerpt, the singer Zarechnaya plans to winter in Svetloledovka, singing to audiences who understand nothing of opera.

Scene use: Use the Theater for staged scenes: a hushed audience, the greenroom, a cold-faced ballerina, a singer with a mischievous streak, a clerk checking tickets. Treat the Troupe as prestigious and strictly run.

Good beats: Odette repairing her music box at night; Vodyanitsa nagging colleagues to attend her shows; a Harbinger or senior official in the audience; Alyosha earning wages backstage; rumours of a ghost in the empty theater at night. Keep Odette disciplined, formal and tired rather than gushing toward fans. Do not invent new ballet plots beyond the excerpted ones.

Tensions that suit canon: Fatui duty against rehearsal time, public persona against private grief, star status against loneliness. Rokot ties and the events of Wraith's Nocturne are spoilers; keep them out of scenes set before the user has reached them.

Examples: Canon examples: the Black Snow Swan premiere preparations (World Quest, 7.0), the daily Korolevskiy Theater's Performance, and the "Spirit Seeker" preview in Winter's Mysterious Silence. Odette's profile and voice-overs add anecdotes about fans, critics and stage-door encounters.

23.comment: Snezhnayan Ballet and Theater: Korolevskiy Troupe
23.content:
A performance troupe based in Snezhnograd that specialises in opera, theater and musical performances. It is very popular in Snezhnayan circles, most notably among the Fatui Harbingers and Mitya. Its named stars are Odette (prima ballerina) and Vodyanitsa (prima donna). Dorofeya, Pashkov and Violetta are listed as former members: Violetta danced, Dorofeya was a singer who retired early, and Pashkov left to be the safety officer of Svetloledovka.

Odette and Vodyanitsa are close friends and colleagues, and the Troupe gives each a daytime role. Their friendly bickering over Odette's overwork is a running thread of the World Quest Variations on Belyi and Chernyi. Open-world NPCs at the Theater include hosts and the ticket-checker Kulish, who seems to be a fan of Odette.

24.comment: Snezhnayan Ballet and Theater: The Korolevskiy Theater
24.content:
A theater in Snezhnograd, in the Everfrozen Earth region of Snezhnaya, where the Korolevskiy Troupe gives its performances. The official map text says that backstage toil matters less here than whether the show can grant the audience a moment's escape into a beautiful illusion. A Meeting Point sits in the dressing room behind the stage. Other spaces include a greenroom, a lobby, an administrative room, Odette's private lounge and a cellar that appears during Winter's Mysterious Silence.

The auditorium holds 312 seats: 44 blue sofas of three, plus four purple three-seat sofas in the lobby. Open-world dialogue is richer after the Mistilteinn quest and once the Theater Meeting Point reaches level 5; characters seen there include Odette, Vodyanitsa, Alyosha, Mitya, Valeriy, Vesna, Tartaglia, Arlecchino and Sandrone.

25.comment: Snezhnayan Ballet and Theater: Black Snow Swan
25.content:
A Korolevskiy Troupe ballet with Odette in the lead; its script excerpts form Polestar Ballet Anthology Vol. 1. Odile, a black snow swan, is ashamed of her dark feathers and begs to be as pure as her white sisters. Their queen, Myrtha, says the colour comes from human love and passion, a poison that binds one to fate, and that tenderness is weakness. Three phantoms will visit Odile on successive nights. In the excerpted ending Odile refuses Myrtha's creed: love, she says, is the blade that cuts fate's snare. At dawn she soars higher than any snow swan.

In Variations on Belyi and Chernyi, a World Quest, Odette and Vodyanitsa discuss the premiere, two weeks away. Odette practised the role as a child but never performed it on stage. She once disliked the black swan, whom she did not want to resemble, but now sympathises and says that in the story the black swan stops trying to fit the flock, flies higher than any white swan and is embraced by the clouds. Because she wants to balance the part with Fatui missions, Vodyanitsa persuades her to let the Traveler plan her schedule as her manager for two weeks.

26.comment: Snezhnayan Ballet and Theater: Polestar Ballet Anthology
26.content:
A four-volume collection of script anthologies from the Korolevskiy Troupe. Vol. 1 contains Black Snow Swan; Vol. 2 The Seabird; Vol. 3 The Envoy; Vol. 4 The Firebird. Vol. 1 comes from finishing Variations on Belyi and Chernyi for the first time; Vols. 2-4 are sold by Moes at Torchlight Books.

The Seabird (Act IV) is set in a country-estate banquet hall: the composer Kostya, dissatisfied with fashionable music, meets Zarechnaya, a singer who left for Snezhnograd with Boris, lost her stage there and has come back only to say goodbye. She has learned to sing for the joy of song. The Envoy opens in the reign of Emperor Monomakh, where a manservant bursts into Viscount Schpekin's banquet with a sealed dispatch from the Zapolyarny Palace and the dancers freeze. The Firebird follows Khramov, third son of Grand Duke Vernov, who guards the golden apple tree and chases the fire-feathered bird Sirin; the Demon King Berstuk and Princess Vaselisa are in the cast.

27.comment: Snezhnayan Ballet and Theater: Spirit Seeker
27.content:
A classic Snezhnayan ballet inherited by Violetta Spessiva's family; Violetta was an acclaimed ballerina at the Theater until a fall left her unable to dance. The sources read do not summarise its plot. In the Archon Quest chapter after Everwinter Without Mercy, a preview of it is held at the Theater, and a group photo of those present, the "Spirit Seeker" Preview Commemorative Photo, becomes a clue item.

The photo's entries describe Theater staff and guests: the ticket-checker Kulish, the host Rampana, the hunter Alyosha, the mercenary Shram, the factory owner Chugunov, Tonia, the Traveler, Odette, Valeriy, Vodyanitsa, Mitya, and the businesspeople Soboleva and Torgov. As the quest proceeds, several entries are updated to record who died in the night. Odette's own entry says she is suspected of having a second identity, Lelek.

28.comment: Snezhnayan Ballet and Theater: Winter's Mysterious Silence
28.content:
In Archon Quest Chapter VII (Wraith's Nocturne, Act II) the Korolevskiy Theater becomes the setting of a closed, wintry mystery. After the preview of "Spirit Seeker", the Traveler and other guests, including Odette, Vodyanitsa, Mitya, Valeriy and Chugunov, wake to find people dead or gone, and a black mist drives them through the building. According to the wiki's summaries Ronova's curse is behind the deaths, and Vodyanitsa's Requiem helps save the Traveler and Mitya.

Afterwards Odette, as Lelek, breaks into the Armory Palace; Ronova's curse takes hold of her and she places her Cor Ignis on the Traveler. The Rokot negotiate clemency but suspend her. She later dances at Signora's tomb and breaks the Cor Ignis. Odette, Vodyanitsa and Alyosha then renovate a place called Rankova Zorya. Treat all of this as Archon Quest spoilers; each character's own entry holds the detail.

key: One Yet to Take a Bow
29.comment: Snezhnayan Ballet and Theater: One Yet to Take a Bow
29.content:
A World Quest about a rumour that eerie music plays in the Korolevskiy Theater at midnight and a ghost's shadow dances on the wall. At night the Traveler finds Odette in the greenroom: the ghost is a broken swan-shaped music box, a childhood gift from her mother, which she repairs in secret in her private lounge because her days are full. She asks for help gathering parts and for silence. She offers the Traveler a reward of redecorating the lounge, but only after repairs, because the ghost keeps visitors away. In the end the box plays again with a ballerina figurine on top.

Post-quest dialogue shows Odette in rehearsal and with Vodyanitsa. For example, she squeezes Vodyanitsa's shows into a packed schedule because Vodyanitsa would otherwise turn up unannounced in her makeup room, and at Podvorye Restaurant she cannot always get her Snowfield dessert. Most such dialogue appears only after the Mistilteinn quest and Theater Meeting Point level 5.

30.comment: Snezhnayan Ballet and Theater: Korolevskiy Theater's Performance
30.content:
A repeatable exploration objective available after Everwinter Without Mercy. Ksenia sells the ticket at the entrance, then a short show plays. Four versions rotate at daily reset: Odette alone, Odette with domovoy dancers, Vodyanitsa preparing her voice, and Odette and Vodyanitsa together. Audience members vary: Arlecchino, Vesna, Mitya, Sandrone and Tartaglia are shown.

Backstage lines show how seriously the Troupe works. Odette plans improvised steps in case a domovoy group number goes wrong, and says a little nervousness helps focus. Vodyanitsa predicts a flawless show. Tartaglia wishes Tonia could have come, and Sandrone remarks that attending was not a waste of time.

31.comment: Snezhnayan Ballet and Theater: Former Troupe Members
31.content: Dorofeya was a rising star and singer with the Korolevskiy Troupe who retired early; she now lives in Snezhnograd on her husband's land holdings and admires Odette's ballet. She warns that audiences adore the flawless stage illusion rather than the performer. Pashkov, a young man, left the Troupe to become the safety officer of Svetloledovka, where he is known for strictness about Prime Ice safety rules.

32.content:
Snezhnayan Script (also: Snezhnaya script, Snezhnayan writing, Nod-Krai script): The Snezhnayan Script is the lettering found on signs, shopfronts, books and documents in Snezhnaya and Nod-Krai. It looks very much like the common script seen elsewhere in Teyvat, with no separate upper and lower case and no punctuation, and it is used almost entirely to spell English and Russian words. Characters just read it as ordinary writing.

The name is the wiki's label rather than an in-world term. It is occasionally also used to write Latin. An item description for a bunker access card, obtained in the world quest Return to Sender, refers to neat Snezhnayan text printed on the card, which gives it a small in-game anchor.

The wiki treats it as the writing system of Snezhnaya including Nod-Krai, and sets it apart from the common script mainly by region and by its Russian-flavoured vocabulary. It is a close relative in look, not a separate language.

Practice: Seen on business signs and labels in Nod-Krai: Voynich Chamber of Commerce, Speranza, Nuts 'N' Nuts, the Flagship, Mead-Boy, and the Rossum Workshop sign, which reads Maszyna.

Deciphered readings from community work include a Northland Bank branch sign in Nod-Krai that appears to read BSK Bank (the wiki suggests this stands for the bank's Russian name), the Curatorium of Secrets sign reading Nefer's, and a protest sign near Omesov. The engraving at the Final Night Cemetery is a tribute to Chudomir the Aarnivalkea. The Nasha Town event signage lists categories such as roulette, candy, ticket and gadget.

Printed items use it too. The Moon-Prayer Night Pamphlet carries a title reading Kuunrukous Night, the book A Brief History of the Pale Starborn has a cover reading V Lyudyakh (likely Russian for 'in people', per the wiki), and the Tier II Bunker Access Card shows the letters MAST and the name A. Z. Kotelnikov, matching the item text that names him as a senior maintenance technician. The statue of the Torchforger at Piramida carries a Latin line, one of the few non-English, non-Russian uses listed.

Regional variation: No dialect or regional variants are documented. It is tied to Snezhnaya and Nod-Krai, while the common script dominates Mondstadt, Liyue and Natlan.

The wiki's listed examples come from Nod-Krai content and items. Do not assume a different hand or style between Snezhnaya proper and Nod-Krai.

Scene use: Use it as set dressing: a sign, label or pamphlet in neat northern lettering, with shop names and short Russian-flavoured words.

Do not invent a grammar, alphabet or sound values for it. If a character reads a sign, keep to what canon supports: it is Snezhnaya's ordinary writing, mostly English and Russian words, and a reader from another nation can generally follow it as they would any foreign shop sign.

33.content:
Vestnik (also: Snezhnaya Vestnik, Vestnik Snezhnoy, Snezhnayan newspaper): The Snezhnaya Vestnik ("Herald") is the newspaper read across Snezhnaya. Copies can be picked up at newspaper stands, typically inside a town's train station. Each issue mixes sensational crime and railway news, official statements, adverts, theatre criticism, serialized fiction and stories sent in by readers. It is comic, gossipy and not always trustworthy, and it shows what ordinary Snezhnayans read while they wait for a train.

The paper is usually just called the Vestnik; the word is Russian for "herald". It is a very public medium: the Transport Bureau, the Snezhnograd Veche and private firms all use its pages, and anyone may submit a manuscript.

Practice: Where it is found: newspaper stands in the train stations of Snezhnaya's towns and cities, and in a few other spots in settlements. Station life and newspaper reading go together; a traveller buys or reads an issue while waiting for the train.

What it prints: (1) news and crime reports, often in a breathless, patriotic tone with appeals to "Her Majesty"; (2) official notices, such as Transport Bureau statements on rail incidents and banned passengers; (3) paid adverts and franchise offers, some of them swindles; (4) health and lifestyle columns; (5) arts criticism, notably the "Today's On Ice" theatre column; (6) serialized fiction; and (7) reader-submitted pieces under the banners "Tales of the Strange and Incredible" and "Snowland Sensations", marked as contributor stories.

How readers take part: the Snezhnograd bulletin board carries a standing call for submissions. Authors whose work is approved are promised a free one-year subscription. Named contributors printed in the paper include Korsakov, Mamontov, Trigorin and Tripolev; Trigorin and Tripolev quarrel over a ballet production in two successive columns.

Tone and conventions: crime stories use pseudonyms ("identified here by the pseudonym..."). Stories that are fiction carry a disclaimer that the paper takes no liability for their accuracy, and one long-running serial is advertised with a pointer to Torchlight Books for the full text. Editors also annotate reprints: a Fontainian travelogue claiming to describe Snezhnaya was printed with bracketed corrections marking its errors, and the editors note that its author never left Fontaine.

Mind-set of the pages: official bodies are praised, ordinary people are told to be wary of scams, and almost every column drifts toward gossip, grievance or conspiracy. The Transport Bureau uses the paper to advise citizens to buy its official delay insurance instead of private policies.

Regional variation: The paper is printed for all of Snezhnaya, but its stories travel with the rails. Snezhnograd readers get capital crime and arts news (the ice-sculpture exhibition, the ballet column, the "Wandering Samurai" arrest). Stands in Morepesok, Flamefeather Valley and Rankova Zorya lean to rural legend, rail incidents and Okurov. Svetloledovka's stand carries insurance and theatre pieces, and an article notes that Prime Ice sculpture commissions went to designers there. Sretomorozsk carries a train derailment investigation and a further instalment of the Reed Miller serial.

Scene use: Use the Vestnik as a prop and as a source of rumour in scenes set in Snezhnayan stations, trains or taverns. A character can overhear someone reading an item aloud, complain about a column, or recall a contributor story. Good uses: an NPC waiting at a stand with a folded issue; a bored traveller quoting a ridiculous health column; a Transport Bureau notice that explains a delay; a reader arguing about the ballet columns.

Guardrails: the paper is not an oracle. Do not let a character treat a Vestnik claim as established lore, and do not invent new articles that give Fatui or Tsaritsa secrets. Keep new items consistent in tone: bureaucratic notice, scam advert, serial fiction or reader letter. Stay with the Snezhnayan voice (formal addresses, pseudonyms, references to Her Majesty), and keep fictional crime stories non-graphic.

Characters from outside Snezhnaya may find the paper charming or baffling. A Snezhnayan can plausibly treat contributor stories as folklore, adverts as warnings, and the Veche or Transport Bureau notices as the voice of authority, without any of them being fully trusted.

Examples: News and notices (Snezhnaya Vestnik, version 7.0):
- The Inazuman "Wandering Samurai" who terrorised Snezhnograd's Downtown District is arrested in an abandoned bakery by the Criminal Investigation Division and Druzhna patrols. The report says he was a bankrupt Ritou merchant who stole armour and a shrine blade, passed through Nod-Krai (where the Curatorium of Secrets exposed him), and Inazuman authorities refuse to recognise him as their citizen, so he awaits judgment under Snezhnayan law.
- A Transport Bureau investigation into freight train I-330, derailed on the Snezhnograd to Novokitezhgrad line, questions whether the conductor's decision to uncouple the freight cars and speed through a landslide was heroism or a breach of safety rules.
- A Transport Bureau notice says a Wild Hunt creature carried a Lightkeeper's lantern along the tundra line between Snezhnograd and Sretomorozsk, and that the Bureau and the Lightkeepers at Piramida are clearing the monsters.
- A second notice bans a grieving Snegovik, Mr. I. N. Ivanov, from the Snezhnograd to Novokitezhgrad trains because his sorrow chills the carriage and makes passengers ill.
- A Veche and Prime Ice Art Alliance exhibition of Prime Ice sculpture is announced as the tsaritsa-era promise of art for everyone, with commissions given to designers in Svetloledovka.
- The investigation of the missing jewel "Star of the Snowfield" is reported with pseudonyms taken from a ballet; the suspect confesses to murder but denies theft.
- A Fatui-funded astronomer reports seeing a crystal palace and creatures on the moon through a giant telescope; the instrument then sets fire to the observatory, and the paper promises a six-issue serial of his letter.

Adverts and columns: Snezhnajoy Insurance sells train-delay, Prime Ice melt and "audience trauma" cover, but a later article reports it refuses claims on technicalities and is under investigation. A franchise offer for "Frosta", described as an upgrade to Fonta, demands ten million Mora. A Society for Traditional Snezhnayan Medicine column insists hot baths are harmful and a woman publicly announces she has left her husband over his refusal to bathe. "Healthguards" columns offer deliberately silly health tips. A grand duke posts a boastful job advert for private guards after his fountain-repainting disaster.

key: Tales of the Strange and Incredible
34.content:
Reader submissions are labelled contributor stories. "Tales of the Strange and Incredible" retells ghost stories and urban legends told as "a friend of a friend": a duke recounting the fire that took his family, a honeymooning couple found dead near Svetloledovka, the Firebird of Okurov that feeds on memories, a lost adventurer saved by a Jack Frost witch who demands a Jack Frost choir, a headless railway attendant wandering the line with a lantern, Volkodlak miners whose find from the ruins of Kitezhgrad is blamed on the curse of Chernabog, and a naturalist who claims a soul-voyage into the age of lizards. "Snowland Sensations" offers a poem to the snowy plains and pseudo-historical essays. Each carries a disclaimer that it may contain fiction.

Two "New Teyvat Chronicles" pieces argue that Decarabian, Al-Ahmar, Remus and Och-Kan are regional echoes of one ruler, Tsar Monomakh, and that the unified ancient ruins found across Teyvat prove his world-spanning realm. They are presented as the author's theory, are full of bad etymology and invented supporting evidence, and should be read as comic crank scholarship. The Okurov and Svetloledovka stories are legends told in the paper, not established history of those places.

key: Seven Impossible Mysteries of Reed Miller
35.content: The paper prints numbered chapters of "The Seven Impossible Mysteries of Reed Miller, Thief Extraordinaire!", with the story of the Platinum Piece shown in Chapters 5 and 11. In the printed extracts a man presenting himself as Grand Duke Brahe Trubetskoy exposes a viscount who took a platinum chess piece and killed his wife; in the later chapter the real grand duke learns that the "envoy" was Reed Miller in disguise, and that Miller has a female companion who calls herself Wagtail. Only fragments of the serial appear in the paper. For the book and the character, see the Reed Miller entries.

36.comment: Vestnik: Vestnik and the Transport Bureau
36.content: The Snezhnaya Royal Railway Transport Bureau uses the paper to issue public statements: a rail-line hazard notice naming a Wild Hunt creature and a Lightkeeper's lantern, a ruling banning a grieving Snegovik from trains, an inquiry into freight train I-330's derailment, and a warning about insurance fraud that promotes its own delay insurance. These notices show how the Bureau speaks to the public: careful, procedural and slightly defensive.
